Wreak

REEK -- from Old English wrecan, 'to drive out, punish, avenge'; the same root as wreck. · verb

Hear It

What It Means

To wreak to cause damage, havoc, or destruction to something, often in the phrase 'wreak havoc'.

A single overturned truck wreaked havoc on rush-hour traffic across the whole downtown grid.

Worked Example

The escaped goat spent one afternoon in the community garden and somehow managed to trample the tomatoes, knock over three trellises, and eat an entire row of lettuce.

That kind of sudden, widespread damage caused by one loose cause -- one goat, one storm, one glitch -- is exactly what it means to wreak havoc.

How Wreak Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

inflict

inflict: to cause something unpleasant to be suffered

unleash

unleash: to release a powerful and often destructive force suddenly

Antonyms

repair

repair: to fix or restore something damaged

forestall

forestall: to prevent something by acting first

How Strong Is It? — inflict → wreak → unleash

inflict vs. wreak

inflict vs. wreak: Inflict is a broad word for causing any unpleasant thing to happen to someone, from a minor inconvenience to real harm. Wreak is stronger and almost always paired with a word like 'havoc' or 'destruction,' picturing large-scale chaos.

unleash vs. wreak

unleash vs. wreak: Unleash is close in strength to wreak, and often appears in similar contexts ('unleash chaos'), though unleash focuses more on suddenly releasing a force, while wreak focuses on the damage that force causes.

The pieces

root — wrek-

Put it together

Put it together: Wreak comes from Old English wrecan, 'to drive out, punish, avenge' -- the same Germanic root behind wreck -- so to wreak damage is, at its root, closely tied to the idea of a punishing, wrecking force.
